title: Transferable prediction of wear and component life

concept.text: The innovation would be a predictive framework that estimates how contacting surfaces lose material and when that wear causes a component to exceed a defined operating tolerance. Its defining advance would be transfer: predictions would remain useful across substantially different materials, contact types and operating conditions without requiring new wear-test calibration for every application. Outputs would include wear depth or volume over time, changes in the dominant wear mechanism, and uncertainty in wear-limited service life.

Wear is an evolving interaction among surface roughness, plastic deformation, fracture, chemical reactions, debris, temperature and lubrication. Their relative importance changes between contacts and can change during a single component’s operation. The supplied review supports treating wear as a coupled, condition-dependent process; it does not establish that every mechanism matters equally in every application. A transferable framework would have to account for these differences rather than assume one wear law applies everywhere.

As a proposed capability, this does not require universally exact prediction from first principles. A useful framework could combine physical, numerical and empirical methods, provided its inputs, calibration history, uncertainty and validated operating domain were explicit. The central test would be whether it predicts independently chosen cases without fitting to their wear outcomes. Wear-limited life would mean time to a specified wear-related endpoint, not a prediction of every possible component failure.

significance.text: Reliable transfer would let engineers estimate wear and tolerance-limited life before building and testing each new component configuration. The supplied review documents simulation’s existing role in reducing experimental time and cost. Extending that usefulness beyond narrowly calibrated conditions could substantially change design comparisons, component qualification and maintenance planning by reducing the amount of case-specific testing needed to make credible predictions. This broader impact is a conditional assessment of the proposed capability.

Conditional downstream possibilities include comparing materials, surface treatments and lubrication choices using predicted service life, and planning inspections or replacement around quantified uncertainty. Bearings, gears, seals and tools could benefit where their relevant mechanisms and operating histories fall within the validated domain. These are proposed applications: success on an initial contact benchmark would not establish readiness across all of those component classes.

The important limit is the distinction between prediction and prevention. Accurate wear forecasts would not themselves eliminate material loss, suppress friction or protect against unrelated failures. Deployment would still require representative loads and environmental histories, defined tolerances and application-specific validation. A component could remain within its wear allowance and nevertheless fail for another reason.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is reliable prediction across changes in material, contact geometry, mechanism and environment without repeatedly determining wear parameters from tests of the target system. The supplied review describes experimentally calibrated models and empirical methods whose usefulness is restricted to their tested conditions or input ranges. Those restrictions explain the transfer challenge; they do not prove that broader prediction or further first-principles progress is impossible.

A central scientific barrier is that the contact being predicted changes as it wears. Evolving geometry and roughness interact with deformation, fracture, debris, temperature, lubrication and chemistry, and the dominant mechanism may change along the way. Predicting accumulated material loss therefore requires more than selecting an initial wear coefficient: the model must remain appropriate as the physical system evolves.

Engineering synthesis: turning these models into credible service-life predictions also requires connecting independently measured starting properties and specified operating histories to a defined tolerance endpoint. Uncertainty must propagate through that calculation rather than appear only as a final error bar. A framework would need to distinguish uncertainty in inputs and parameters from limitations in its representation of the wear mechanisms, and identify conditions outside its demonstrated domain.

The evidence also leaves an important scope boundary. The supplied review concentrates on mechanically dominated wear. Although it discusses chemical effects, it does not comprehensively establish predictive transfer into chemically dominated regimes. Extending the innovation to those regimes would require additional evidence and validation.

current_state.text: Paweł Pawlus and Rafał Reizer’s “A State of the Art on Mechanically Dominated Methods of Wear Modelling,” published online on 8 September 2025, documents physical, numerical and empirical approaches already used in engineering. The supplied evidence review identifies experimentally compared finite-element models and applications involving cam-followers, gears, bearings, cylinder/piston-ring systems and wheel–rail contacts. These establish useful existing modelling capabilities within particular applications and assumptions.

The same review describes different wear laws, experimental calibration needs and restrictions on empirical predictions outside tested conditions. Its discussion supports broad transfer across mechanisms and operating conditions as an outstanding challenge at publication. That conclusion is a synthesis of the documented limitations, not an exhaustive proof that every available model fails to transfer. The supplied material does not demonstrate the full capability proposed here.

Uncertainty analysis is already part of wear modelling: the supplied evidence includes discussion of uncertainty in wear coefficients. That is relevant groundwork, but it does not demonstrate calibrated probability intervals for the time at which independently chosen components exceed their wear tolerances. Likewise, existing validation of a model in a particular application does not establish transfer to other mechanisms or environments.

The supplied assessment rests on partial HTML and PDF extractions of this review; both were truncated at 120,000 extracted characters. The validated review reports that document identity and the relevant technical discussions were available despite that truncation. This supports the conclusions drawn from those passages, while limiting claims about comprehensive coverage. No subsequent search results were supplied, so developments between 8 September 2025 and the review’s stated assessment date of 1 November 2026 remain unassessed. Retrieval of the artifacts on 11 November 2026 does not establish a later technical update.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed first milestone: before observing held-out wear-test results, predict wear depth or volume, dominant mechanism transitions and a probability distribution for end-of-tolerance life. The independently chosen suite should include sliding, rolling and abrasive contacts, span at least two material families, and vary humidity or contamination. Predictions should use independently measured initial material and surface properties together with specified operating histories, with no wear-test retuning on held-out cases.
completion_criteria.label: Prospective wear and lifetime predictions transfer without held-out wear-test retuning

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evaluation rules should be registered before the tests. They should specify the contact suite, tolerance endpoints, wear measurement times and locations, treatment of measurements near zero or below detection limits, and how mechanism transitions will be identified and scored. A factor-of-two target for wear predictions is a candidate first milestone, not an established standard. Its scoring rule must make clear which measurements must meet it and how performance across the suite will be aggregated.
completion_criteria.label: Preregistered evaluation rules define wear scoring across the contact suite

completion_criteria.text: Proposed lifetime criteria should assess both interval coverage and sharpness: uncertainty intervals should contain the observed tolerance-crossing times at the declared frequency while remaining narrow enough to inform decisions. Arbitrarily wide intervals should not count as successful prediction. Evaluation should also define how to handle components that do not reach their tolerance endpoint during the experiment.
completion_criteria.label: Lifetime intervals achieve declared coverage with decision-useful sharpness

completion_criteria.text: The supplied review grounds the need for experimental validation, but it does not prescribe these numerical thresholds or benchmark details. A convincing demonstration would compare prospective predictions with subsequent measurements and disclose the assumptions, calibration dependencies and operating restrictions that determine where the results apply.
completion_criteria.label: Prospective predictions undergo experimental validation with applicability limits disclosed

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements include enough information about model versions, prior calibration data, input measurements, operating histories, protocols and results for independent investigators to repeat the assessment. Replication by another laboratory and testing on additional unseen contacts would strengthen the claim. Even successful finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within a stated domain, not literal universality or qualification for every machine.
completion_criteria.label: Assessment is independently reproducible with demonstrated domain limits stated

related_concepts.text: MEC-12, “Predictive mechanics of real, evolving surface contacts,” is closely connected because many wear predictions depend on the forces, deformation and geometry of the contact. MEC-12 addresses contact behaviour; MEC-11 extends the problem to material loss, mechanism changes and wear-limited life. Contact prediction is an important input to many wear models, but it does not by itself determine wear chemistry, debris evolution or the resulting service life. This distinction follows from the supplied roster and research.

MEC-02, “Service-life superlubricity in ordinary machine contacts,” overlaps through friction, lubrication and contact durability. Its objective is to sustain exceptionally low friction over useful service life; MEC-11 seeks transferable predictions of wear, including in contacts that do not achieve superlubricity. Low-friction operation can change the conditions governing wear, but friction and material loss are distinct outcomes. This is a conceptual comparison based on the supplied roster.

MEC-04, “Ambient fatigue immunity in bulk structural metals,” shares the broader objective of improving component durability. Its focus is resistance to fatigue damage, while MEC-11 concerns prediction of contact-driven material loss and wear-related tolerance limits. Where fatigue contributes to contact damage, the subjects can interact, but neither fatigue immunity nor accurate wear prediction establishes total component reliability. This is a conceptual comparison based on the supplied roster.

MEC-13, “General-purpose synthesis of practical mechanisms,” could conditionally use transferable wear and lifetime predictions to evaluate proposed mechanisms against durability requirements. MEC-13 concerns generating practical mechanisms; MEC-11 supplies a possible predictive capability for assessing their contacting parts. Successful mechanism synthesis would not establish transferable wear prediction, and wear prediction alone would not generate a complete mechanism. This is a proposed relationship based on the supplied roster.

unresolved_issues: No supplied search results establish whether developments after 8 September 2025 changed the assessment by 1 November 2026 or the 11 November 2026 retrieval date.
The partial source extractions support the reported passages but do not establish complete coverage of the underlying review.
Transfer into chemically dominated wear regimes remains outside the comprehensively supported scope of the supplied source.
The benchmark still needs concrete material families, contact geometries, operating histories, tolerance endpoints, transition labels, and numerical interval-coverage and sharpness requirements.
The factor-of-two scoring rule needs a precise treatment of near-zero wear, detection limits, aggregation and acceptable failures across the suite.
The practical domain over which a successful benchmark could justify component qualification or maintenance decisions remains to be demonstrated.

brief.title: Predicting wear and how long parts will last
possible: Engineers could predict how much material a part will lose and when that loss will make it too worn to operate within specified limits. The same framework could work across different materials, contacts and operating conditions without needing fresh wear tests for every application.
why: Designers could compare materials, surface treatments and lubricants with less testing of each new configuration. Maintenance teams could plan inspections and replacement around predicted remaining life and its uncertainty.

sources.showed: Their review describes wear models used in engineering, including comparisons with experiments. It identifies dependence on experimental calibration and limits on predictions beyond tested conditions.
sources.cited_for: Existing models can help within particular applications, while broader transfer remains a challenge.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate predictions that transfer across materials, wear processes and environments without fresh fitting.

sources.who: Zongshuo Li, Markus Meurer and Thomas Bergs
sources.showed: In experiments with 20 milling tools, a machine learning model estimated wear better when it included cutting conditions. It was tested on cutting settings absent from training.
sources.quote:
The results consistently highlight our
approach’s advantage over conventional models that omit cutting conditions, maintaining superior performance irrespective of the stability of the
wear development or the limitation of the training dataset.
sources.cited_for: Including operating conditions can improve wear estimates under new cutting settings.
sources.not_established: Estimating milling-tool wear does not establish future lifetime predictions across different materials and contact types.

sources.who: Tobias Brink, Lucas Frérot and Jean-François Molinari
sources.showed: They built a model without fitted parameters for dry sliding of brittle materials, where bonds between surfaces cause particles to detach. Comparison with experiments gave qualitative agreement.
sources.quote:
A comparison
with an experimental work by Kim et al. (1986) that contains suﬃcient data to feed our model yields some
qualitative agreement
sources.cited_for: Material properties and surface measurements can support wear modelling without fitted wear parameters.
sources.not_established: Qualitative agreement in this restricted wear process does not establish accurate wear amounts or transferable component lifetimes.

sources.who: Ramin Aghababaei, Derek H Warner and Jean-Francois Molinari
sources.showed: Simulations of atoms showed that the size of bonds between surface bumps controls whether the bumps smooth out or fracture into debris. A mathematical model predicted this change in simulations and experiments.
sources.quote: This length scale provides a critical adhesive junction size, where bigger junctions produce wear debris by fracture while smaller ones smooth out plastically.
sources.cited_for: Physical models can predict a change between distinct wear processes.
sources.not_established: Predicting what happens at individual surface bumps does not establish accumulated wear or lifetime across whole components.

shown: Researchers have demonstrated pieces of the capability: better wear estimates under new milling conditions, a model without fitted wear parameters, and predictions of how debris forms. Pawlus and Reizer’s review also documents models compared with experiments in specific engineering applications.
missing: Predictions must transfer across materials, contact shapes and environments without fitting to wear results from each new case.
Models must track how changing surfaces, debris, heat and lubrication alter the process causing material loss.
Lifetime predictions must connect measured starting properties and operating histories to a defined wear limit, carrying uncertainty throughout.
Independent experiments must establish where predictions remain useful and where they cease to apply.

milestones.label: Wear and lifetime predictions transfer to unseen contacts
milestones.explanation: Blind tests would have to predict wear, changes in wear processes and lifetime probabilities across sliding, rolling and abrasive contacts without refitting. Varied materials and environments would test transfer.

milestones.label: Evaluation rules are fixed before testing
milestones.explanation: Rules would have to define contacts, wear limits, measurement schedules and scoring, including barely detectable wear and changes in wear processes. This would make success across the test suite clear.

milestones.label: Lifetime ranges are reliable and useful
milestones.explanation: Predicted lifetime ranges would have to contain observed lifetimes as often as promised while staying narrow enough for decisions. Rules for parts that never reach their wear limit would prevent misleading scores.

milestones.label: Experiments confirm predictions within stated limits
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to agree with predictions made before testing, with assumptions, prior fitting and operating restrictions disclosed. This would establish where engineers could use the results.

milestones.label: Independent researchers can repeat the assessment
milestones.explanation: Enough model, input and test information would have to be shared for independent researchers to repeat the assessment. Replication and further unseen contacts would strengthen confidence in its stated range.

uncertain: Transfer to conditions where chemical reactions dominate wear remains an open question.
A factor-of-two wear target is only a proposal; acceptable errors, barely detectable wear and combined scores still need precise rules.
The required reliability and width of lifetime ranges, and the breadth needed for maintenance decisions, remain to be defined.

page.title: Transferable prediction of wear and wear-limited life
page.definition: A model predicts material loss at contacting surfaces and the time when that loss exceeds a specified component tolerance, with quantified uncertainty. The same framework transfers across materials, contact geometries and operating environments without fitting to wear measurements from each target application; the scope is mechanically dominated wear.

goal.need: A global assessment published in 2017 attributed approximately 16 EJ, or 3% of world energy consumption, to remanufacturing worn parts and spare equipment because of wear and wear-related failures. Wear simulation addresses experimental time and cost, but the 2025 review documents experimental calibration and restrictions on empirical predictions outside tested conditions.

completion.title: Independent experiments validate transferred wear and life predictions without target wear calibration.
completion.criterion: An independent laboratory tests a frozen model on a suite spanning at least two material families, two contact geometries and two operating environments. Wear trajectories and time to a specified wear tolerance are predicted before testing, without fitting to target wear measurements. Every case meets application-owner numerical limits for wear error, life error, uncertainty-interval coverage and maximum interval width. Limits, sample sizes and operating histories are published before prediction. Success establishes the tested domain only.
completion.set_by: Atlas; an operational definition pending an externally specified cross-application benchmark.
completion.basis: Searches of ASTM G99, STLE reports, NIST wear-prediction work, Fraunhofer projects, i-TRIBOMAT and PHM-AP rules found no completion test covering wear and wear-limited life across materials, geometries and environments without target wear calibration. Two instances of each variation are the minimum needed to demonstrate transfer. Application owners must supply numerical acceptance limits; no common values were found.

milestones.title: A contact model predicts both plastic smoothing and fracture-induced wear debris.
milestones.criterion: A model predicts the transition between two observed adhesive-contact outcomes: plastic smoothing and particle formation by fracture. Its predicted transition is compared with atomistic simulations and experiments. Aghababaei, Warner and Molinari reported this comparison in 2016. This establishes a mechanism-level demonstration; it does not establish accumulated component wear or life.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; searches of STLE, ASTM and NIST material found no adopted mechanism-prediction attainment criterion. The demonstration is drawn from adhesive-wear research.

milestones.title: A ceramic-wear model predicts wear within one order of magnitude across materials and conditions.
milestones.criterion: Predicted ceramic wear lies between 0.1 and 10 times measured wear across the evaluated materials and operating conditions. Hsu and Shen reported this resolution in 2004; it is used here as a retrospective research benchmark. Separately, Brink and colleagues' 2021 parameter-free sliding model reproduced the wear ranking of three ceramics against rolling-contact experiments, with substantial differences in absolute wear and using measured steady-state roughness.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; no adopted quantitative transfer milestone was found. The numerical resolution is Hsu and Shen's reported research result, not a NIST acceptance standard.

milestones.title: A cutter-wear model reaches a PHM-AP 2025 top-six place on three hidden evaluation datasets.
milestones.criterion: Rank among the first six teams under the challenge's combined per-dataset ranks for root mean square error, mean absolute percentage error and R². Models use six training datasets and three hidden evaluation datasets covering repeated cuts, with the first available wear label supplied. The official winning entry recorded 7.878% mean absolute percentage error and R² = 0.904. These are competition results, not peer-reviewed validation of component life.
milestones.set_by: PHM-AP 2025 Data Challenge organizers, published competition and scoring rules; the test concerns cutter flank wear.
milestones.threshold_quote: The top six teams will receive award prizes

milestones.title: A tool-wear model lowers estimation error on unseen cutting settings without target retraining.
milestones.criterion: Estimate maximum flank-wear width on tools operated at cutting settings withheld from training, with lower average root mean square error than the otherwise identical model omitting cutting settings. Li and colleagues evaluated 20 tools and 454 milling operations. In the eight-setting evaluation using the first 16 tools, including cutting settings reduced average error by 22.3%. Inputs included contemporaneous sensor signals; this demonstrates wear-state estimation within one tool–workpiece system.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; no industrial acceptance threshold for this transfer stage was found. The comparator and evaluation design come from Li and colleagues' published study.

milestones.title: An independent laboratory validates wear-limited life in one component application.
milestones.criterion: For one component application under changed operating conditions, an independent laboratory verifies predictions made before wear testing of the time to a specified wear tolerance. No target wear measurements are used to fit the model. Life-error limits, uncertainty coverage, maximum interval width, sample size and treatment of specimens not reaching the tolerance are fixed by the application owner before prediction. The opened sources do not establish this result with those conditions.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; searches of STLE, NIST, Fraunhofer, i-TRIBOMAT and PHM-AP material found no published acceptance test for this pre-completion result.

not_found: No externally defined completion benchmark was found for transfer of both wear and wear-limited-life predictions without target wear calibration.
No common numerical requirements were found for prediction error, uncertainty coverage, interval width or the breadth of a transfer benchmark.
No independent component-life validation satisfying the stated completion conditions was found in the searched material.
The NIST abstract does not state its dataset size; the publisher's full article could not be opened.
The full text of Critical length scale controls adhesive wear mechanisms could not be retrieved from PMC, Nature or EPFL; its institutional abstract was accessible.

results.finding: Across 16 tools, including cutting settings reduced average maximum flank-wear estimation RMSE by 22.3%.
results.detail: Eight cutting-parameter sets were held out in turn. The models used contemporaneous sensor signals from one tool–workpiece system.
results.quote:
The inclusion of cutting parameters sig-
nificantly enhances the test model’s performance, yielding a
22.3 % improvement in RMSE and a 3.8 % increase in the coef-
ficient of determination R2 on average over the reference model.

results.finding: For 3 ceramics, predicted wear coefficients were at least 2–3 orders of magnitude above measurements.
results.detail: The model reproduced the wear-resistance ranking, but compared sliding predictions with rolling-contact experiments and used measured steady-state roughness.
results.quote:
Apart from this, Fig. 6(c) shows that our wear coeﬃcients are at least
two to three orders of magnitude higher than the experimental ones (kexp = 6· 10−7 to 1.5· 10−3), although
this is expected since the experiment was a rolling friction setup, which often has such a large diﬀerence
in k compared to sliding friction setups (Hokkirigawa, 1991).

results.finding: An adhesive-contact model predicts the transition between two wear mechanisms; the number of simulations and experimental cases is not stated.
results.detail: The model was compared with atomistic simulations and compiled AFM experiments; it predicted the experimental mechanism in almost every case.
results.quote: A simple analytic model is formulated to predict the transition in both the simulation results and experiments.

results.finding: Ceramic wear prediction across materials and conditions achieved ±1 order of magnitude; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The abstract reports a predictive capability across a range of materials and operating conditions using contact severity and material-property normalization.
results.quote: Finally, we address the issue across a range of materials and operating condition using a concept of contact severity and material property normalization to achieve a predictive capability of ± one order of magnitude over the range of materials and operating conditions.

results.finding: Lone warrior’s cutter-wear model placed 1st across three hidden evaluation datasets.
results.detail: The official final leaderboard reports 7.878% MAPE and R² of 0.904. Rankings combine per-dataset RMSE, MAPE and R² ranks; the challenge used six training datasets and supplied the first available evaluation wear label.
